items.title: Section: Before the Five Contemplations — Three Preliminary Reflections on Karma, Shared Suffering, and the Śrāvaka's Own Example

items.zh: 謂諸菩薩猛利無間種種長時從他怨害所生眾苦現在前時，應如是學：如此是我自業過耳，由我先世自造種種不淨業故，今受如是種種苦果。我今於此無義利苦若不忍者，復為當來大苦因處。我若於此大苦因法隨順轉者，便為於己自作非愛，便為於己自生結縛，便為於己自興怨害，非是於他。又自他身所有諸行，一切皆用性苦為體。彼無知故，於我身中性苦體上更增其苦；我既有知，何宜於彼性苦體上重加其苦。又諸聲聞多分唯修自義利行，尚不應起能生自他眾苦不忍，何況我今正為勤修他義利行而生不忍。
items.en: When intense, unrelenting, varied, and long-lasting suffering arising from another's hostility and harm presents itself, bodhisattvas should train in this way: "This is simply my own karmic fault. Because I myself created various impure actions in past lives, I now receive this kind of painful result. If I fail to endure this meaningless, worthless suffering now, it will only become the cause of great suffering yet to come. If I now go along with this cause of great suffering, I only create something genuinely unwelcome for myself, only bind myself in further affliction, only bring hostility and harm upon myself — not upon anyone else." Furthermore, every activity of both my own body and another's body has, as its very essence, the nature of suffering. Out of sheer ignorance, the other person only adds further suffering onto a body already suffering by its very nature; since I already know better, how could it possibly be fitting for me to pile still more suffering onto a body that is, by nature, already suffering? Furthermore, śrāvakas, for the most part, cultivate practice purely for their own benefit, and yet even they should not give rise to intolerance that produces further suffering for both self and other — how much less should I, who am now diligently cultivating practice for the benefit of others, give rise to such intolerance?

items.zh: 菩薩如是正思擇已，勤修五想，於怨親中、劣等勝品、有樂有苦、具德具失諸有情所，能忍一切怨害之苦。云何五想？一、宿生親善想，二、隨順唯法想，三、無常想，四、苦想，五、攝受想。云何菩薩於有怨害諸有情所，修習宿生親善之想？

items.title: Section: The First Contemplation — Every Enemy Was Once Your Own Mother, Father, or Sibling

items.zh: 謂諸菩薩應如是學：非易可得少分有情，經歷長世昔餘生中，未曾為我若父、若母、兄弟、姊妹、親教、軌範、尊似尊等。如是如理正思惟故，於有怨害諸有情所捨怨憎想，住親善想。依親善想，於諸怨害悉能堪忍。
items.en: Bodhisattvas should train in this way: "It would be no easy thing to find even a small handful of beings who, across the long span of countless past lives, have never once been my father, my mother, my brother, my sister, my ordination preceptor, my instructing teacher, or an honoured elder to me." Through this kind of genuine, principled reflection, bodhisattvas set aside any sense of hostility or resentment towards beings who have done them harm, and abide instead in a sense of genuine kinship. Relying on this sense of kinship, they are able to endure every kind of hostility and harm.

items.zh: 云何菩薩於有怨害諸有情所，修習隨順唯法之想？

items.title: Section: The Second Contemplation — There Was Never Really "Someone" Doing the Harming

items.zh: 謂諸菩薩應如是學：依託眾緣，唯行唯法，此中都無我及有情、命者、生者，是其能罵、能瞋、能打、能弄、能訶，或是所罵、所瞋、所打、所弄、所訶。如是如理正思惟故，於有怨害諸有情所捨有情想，住唯法想。依唯法想，於諸怨害悉能堪忍。
items.en: Bodhisattvas should train in this way: "Arising in dependence on manifold conditions, there is only impersonal activity, only impersonal phenomena; within all this there is no fixed self, no abiding being, no life-possessor, no producer of anything at all — no one who scolds, who grows angry, who strikes, who mocks, who reproaches; and no one who is scolded, made angry at, struck, mocked, or reproached." Through this kind of genuine, principled reflection, bodhisattvas set aside the notion of "a being" doing harm, and abide instead in the recognition of mere impersonal phenomena. Relying on this recognition, they are able to endure every kind of hostility and harm.

items.zh: 云何菩薩於有怨害諸有情所，修無常想？

items.title: Section: The Third and Fourth Contemplations — Already Dying Moment by Moment, and Already Suffering by Nature

items.zh: 謂諸菩薩應如是學：諸有有情若生若長，一切無常，皆是死法。極報怨者，謂斷彼命。是諸有情命念念斷，智者何緣復欲更斷。如是生死性無常法諸有情上，其有智者尚不應起有染濁心，況當以手、塊杖加害，何況一切永斷其命。如是如理正思惟故，捨常堅想，安住無常不堅固想。依無常想，於諸怨害悉能堪忍。云何菩薩於有怨害諸有情所，修習苦想？謂諸菩薩應如是觀：若諸有情大興盛者，尚為三苦常所隨逐，所謂行苦、壞苦、苦苦，況諸有情住衰損者。如是觀已，應如是學：我今於此苦常隨逐諸有情所，應勤方便令離眾苦，不應於彼重加其苦。
items.en: Bodhisattvas should train in this way: "All beings, whether just born or already grown, are entirely impermanent, subject in every case to death. The most extreme act of vengeance one could take is to end another's life — yet these beings' lives are already ending, moment by moment, on their own; why would anyone wise wish to end them further? Given that the very nature of birth and death is already impermanence itself, even a wise person should not give rise to even a defiled thought towards such beings, let alone actually harm them with a hand, a stone, or a rod — how much less end their life entirely?" ... Bodhisattvas should reflect in this way: "Even beings of great flourishing and prosperity are still constantly pursued by the three kinds of suffering — the suffering of conditioned existence itself, the suffering of change, and the suffering of outright pain — how much more so beings already living in decline and hardship." Having reflected in this way, they should further train: "Towards these beings, constantly pursued by suffering, I should diligently apply skilful means to free them from suffering, not add further suffering onto them."

items.zh: 如是如理正思惟故，斷滅樂想，生起苦想。依此苦想，於諸怨害悉能堪忍。云何菩薩於有怨害諸有情所，修攝受想？

items.title: Section: The Fifth Contemplation — Embracing Every Being as One's Own Kin — Patience Towards Hostility and Harm Closes

items.zh: 謂諸菩薩應如是學：我為一切有情之類發菩提心，攝受一切有情之類皆為親眷，我應為彼作諸義利。我今不應本於有情欲作義利，而當於彼不忍怨害，作非義利。如是如理正思惟故，於有怨害諸有情所滅除他想，住攝受想。依攝受想，於諸怨害悉能堪忍。云何名忍？自無憤勃，不報他怨，亦不隨眠流注恒續，故名為忍。是名菩薩耐他怨害忍。
items.en: Bodhisattvas should train in this way: "I gave rise to the aspiration for awakening for the sake of every kind of being, embracing every kind of being as my own kin; I ought to act for their genuine benefit. Having originally resolved to act for beings' benefit, I should not now, faced with their hostility, become intolerant and act instead for their harm." Through this kind of genuine, principled reflection, bodhisattvas dissolve the sense of the other as separate, and abide instead in a sense of genuine embrace. Relying on this sense of embrace, they are able to endure every kind of hostility and harm. What is meant by patience? Being personally free of indignant anger, not retaliating against another's hostility, and not letting it settle into a continuously flowing undercurrent of resentment — this is what is called patience. This is called a bodhisattva's patience towards others' hostility and harm.

blocks.text: How does one actually endure harm? The treatise offers five contemplations. A short passage (0523b15) is untranslated.

"This is simply my own karmic fault: because I created impure actions in past lives, I now receive this." Venerable Miào Jìng tells of Śīlabhadra, whose illness Mañjuśrī traced to a past life as a careless king. And: retaliating plants seeds of future enmity (Master Cháng Bǎi). Even śrāvakas, seeking only their own liberation, practise patience; how much more a bodhisattva.

"It would be no easy thing to find even a few beings who, across countless past lives, have never been my father, mother, sibling, teacher." Master Cháng Bǎi: "In your water is me; in my water is you."

"There is only activity, only phenomena; no self, no one who harms, no one harmed." Master Cháng Bǎi: like being bumped by an empty boat; if someone calls you stupid, there is no "stupid" in the word itself.
"The most extreme act of vengeance is to end another's life; yet these beings' lives are already ending, moment by moment. Why would I take it?" And beings are "suffering by nature"; why add to it?

"I gave rise to the aspiration for awakening for the sake of every being, embracing every being as my own kin. I ought to help them, not harm them." Venerable Miào Jìng: see that person as oneself. Master Cháng Bǎi: like one hand hurting the other.

"What is patience? No inner outburst, no retaliation, and no latent resentment continuing to flow on." Venerable Miào Jìng: even with afflictions present, if they do not stir, it can be called patience.

quiz.q: When suffering from others' hostility arises, what is the bodhisattva's first reflection?
options: this is simply my own karmic fault — past impure deeds now bring this result
quiz.why: "This is simply my own karmic fault. Because I myself created various impure actions in past lives, I now receive this kind of painful result." Venerable Miào Jìng: so when suffering, one blames neither heaven nor others — it is past causes bearing present fruit.

quiz.q: On "my own karmic fault," whose story does Venerable Miào Jìng tell?
options: Śīlabhadra, suffering from a wind disorder, was told by Mañjuśrī that as a king in a past life he had mistreated his people, and must wait three years to teach the Yogācārabhūmi to a monk from China
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: Śīlabhadra had a wind disorder. Mañjuśrī told him that in a past life as king he had not cared for his people but mistreated them, and that in three years a monk would come from China to whom he should teach the Yogācārabhūmi.

quiz.q: What image does Master Cháng Bǎi use for beings having been one another's kin?
options: "in your water there is me, in my water there is you"; regard all men as one's father and all women as one's mother
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: think of all men as my father and all women as my mother; "in your water is me, in my water is you." Once enemies are seen as kin, there is nothing one cannot bear.

quiz.q: On the contemplation of mere phenomena, what image does Master Cháng Bǎi use for why anger is unnecessary?
options: like being struck by an empty boat
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: it is like being bumped by an empty boat. If someone calls you stupid, there is no "stupid" within the word itself — once you see this, you can let go.

quiz.q: What is the reflection of the contemplation of impermanence?
options: beings' lives are already ending moment by moment — why would the wise wish to end them further?
quiz.why: "The most extreme act of vengeance is to end another's life — yet these beings' lives are already ending, moment by moment; why would anyone wise wish to end them further?" Master Cháng Bǎi: there is death at the end of a lifetime and moment-to-moment death — both are "subject to death."

quiz.q: The contemplation of embracing: "embracing all beings as one's own kin." How do the lectures describe the relationship?
options: Miào Jìng: see the harmful person and the bodhisattva as one body; Cháng Bǎi: like the hand naturally brushing a mosquito off one's own foot — beings are one's own body
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: see that person as oneself — the harmful person and the bodhisattva are one body. Master Cháng Bǎi: like a hand naturally brushing away a mosquito biting one's own foot; beings are my own body.

options: no inner outburst, no retaliation, and no latent resentment flowing on
quiz.why: "What is called patience? No inner outburst, no retaliation, and no latent resentment continuing to flow on — this is patience." Master Cháng Bǎi: three marks — no anger oneself, no retaliation, no grudge held in the heart.
